uncertainties.what: Whether the earcut.hpp revision you are targeting has the triangle-bbox fast-reject inside isEar (added upstream in earcut.js 2.2.3 and ported) or the older plain loop.
uncertainties.alternatives: Both forms are given in the isEar pseudocode. They are output-identical: the bbox test with inclusive >=/<= is a strict superset of the region where pointInTriangle can return true, so it can only skip work, never change acceptance. Pick either; prefer the bbox form to match current upstream.
uncertainties.confidence: high that they are output-equivalent; medium on which one is literally in your target file

uncertainties.what: Exact form of pointInTriangle: `(cx-px)*(ay-py) - (ax-px)*(cy-py) >= 0` (earcut 2.x) versus `(cx-px)*(ay-py) >= (ax-px)*(cy-py)` (earcut 3.x refactor).
uncertainties.alternatives: I reported the 2.x subtract-then-compare form, which is what the C++ header-only port (2.2.x) uses. If you are targeting a 3.x-synced port, switch to the two-product comparison. The two differ only when the subtraction underflows/rounds to exactly 0 with opposite-sign operands — extremely rare but real.
uncertainties.confidence: medium-high

uncertainties.what: Whether the bbox pass in operator() uses std::min/std::max calls or explicit if-comparisons (earcut.js uses `if (x < minX) minX = x;`).
uncertainties.alternatives: I reported `std::min<double>` / `std::max<double>` with explicit template arguments, which is what the C++ port uses. Both give identical results for non-NaN input; std::min returns the first argument on ties. No output difference for finite coordinates.
uncertainties.confidence: high

uncertainties.what: Whether operator() hoists `double x; double y;` above the loop (declared once and reused inside the bbox do/while) as I show.
uncertainties.alternatives: Purely stylistic; declaring them inside the loop is semantically identical. No output impact.
uncertainties.confidence: high on semantics, medium on the literal declaration placement

uncertainties.what: Whether the arena sizing line is exactly `nodes.reset(len * 3 / 2)` and the reserve is exactly `indices.reserve(len + points[0].size())`.
uncertainties.alternatives: Possible variants: `nodes.reset(len * 3 / 2)` vs a different multiplier. This only affects allocation, never the emitted index sequence, so it is safe to approximate if you cannot confirm.
uncertainties.confidence: medium

uncertainties.what: Whether earcutLinked contains any iteration counter / bailout.
uncertainties.alternatives: I am confident it does not — the only progress detection is the `ear == stop` lap check. Some third-party forks add an iteration cap; upstream mapbox does not.
uncertainties.confidence: high

uncertainties.what: The C++ bbox being computed over the post-eliminateHoles linked list (thus including hole vertices) rather than over the outer ring only as in earcut.js.
uncertainties.alternatives: If your reference implementation is actually a JS-faithful port, the bbox would be over ring 0 only, computed from the input coordinates before/independently of hole merging. This materially changes inv_size and therefore z-order hashing results for holed polygons with >80 total vertices. Worth verifying against one holed test case with >80 vertices before locking it in — it is the single most likely place for a byte-level divergence.
uncertainties.confidence: medium-high that the C++ port walks the merged linked list

uncertainties.what: Whether earcut.hpp 2.2.4's findHoleBridge tie-break is `(p->x > m->x || sectorContainsSector(m, p))` (ungated) or `(p->x > m->x || (p->x == m->x && sectorContainsSector(m, p)))` (gated, as in earcut.js).
uncertainties.alternatives: I believe the C++ header dropped the `p->x == m->x &&` guard when the JS change was ported, while earcut.js keeps it. If your reference build is earcut.hpp, use the UNGATED form (which is also what the task statement quotes). If your reference is earcut.js 2.2.x/3.x, use the GATED form. The two differ only when tan ties exactly AND p->x < m->x, which requires collinear-with-the-ray candidates — rare but reachable on axis-aligned/grid data.
uncertainties.confidence: medium — high confidence the ungated form is in the .hpp, high confidence the gated form is in the .js

uncertainties.what: Exact revision boundary for eliminateHole V2 vs V3 (`return outerNode == bridge ? filteredBridge : outerNode;` vs `filterPoints(bridgeReverse, ...); return filterPoints(bridge, bridge->next);`).
uncertainties.alternatives: V2 appeared with 2.2.0; V3 replaced it in 2.2.3 (upstream JS made the same change and carried it into 3.x). The residual comment "Check if input node was removed by the filtering" above a plain `return filterPoints(bridge, bridge->next);` is the V3 fingerprint. If your target is earcut.hpp 2.2.0/2.2.1/2.2.2, use V2 — note V2 also filters `bridge` BEFORE `bridgeReverse`, the opposite order from V3.
uncertainties.confidence: medium-high for V3 being the 2.2.4 text; medium for the exact 2.2.3 boundary

uncertainties.what: The 2.2.0/2.2.1 intermediate form of findHoleBridge's hole-touches-segment handling.
uncertainties.alternatives: Three known forms: (i) 2.1.x — inner `if (x == hx) { if (hy == p->y) return p; if (hy == p->next->y) return p->next; }` placed BEFORE `m = ...`, plus a post-loop `if (hx == qx) return m->prev;`; (ii) an intermediate with the same inner block but post-loop `if (hx == qx) return m;`; (iii) 2.2.x/2.2.4 — the single inner `if (x == hx) return m;` placed AFTER `m = ...`, with no post-loop check. Form (iii) is what I report as the earcut.hpp 2.2.4 body. The `m->prev` vs `m` difference in the older post-loop check is the single easiest thing to get wrong.
uncertainties.confidence: medium

uncertainties.what: Whether earcut.hpp 2.2.4's eliminateHoles sort comparator is plain `a->x < b->x` or upstream's compareXYSlope (x, then y, then (next.y-y)/(next.x-x) slope).
uncertainties.alternatives: I am fairly confident earcut.hpp 2.2.4 has the plain lambda `return a->x < b->x;` and that compareXYSlope is an earcut.js-only change that postdates the last .hpp release. If you observe hole-order behaviour that plain-x cannot explain (specifically: two holes meeting at a shared leftmost vertex being handled consistently), your reference has compareXYSlope — port it as `std::sort` with a strict-weak `<` derived from the three-key comparison.
uncertainties.confidence: medium-high

uncertainties.what: Whether the 3.x-era `if (equals(hole, p)) return p;` pre-check and the in-loop `if (equals(hole, p->next)) return p->next;` exist in earcut.hpp 2.2.4's findHoleBridge.
uncertainties.alternatives: I believe they do NOT — they are an earcut.js 3.0 addition. If present in your reference, the pre-check runs before the do/while and the in-loop check is the first arm of an if/else-if chain whose else-if is the `hy <= p->y && ...` test (so a node satisfying equals() short-circuits past the ray test entirely).
uncertainties.confidence: medium-high

uncertainties.what: Whether filterPoints in 2.2.4 opens with a `if (!start) return start;` null guard.
uncertainties.alternatives: The body definitely begins with `if (!end) end = start;`. A preceding null guard exists in some revisions (and is harmless to add, since eliminateHole never passes null in practice). It cannot change output for well-formed input.
uncertainties.confidence: medium

uncertainties.what: Exact placement of `vertices += len;` within linkedList (before vs after the trailing-duplicate removal block).
uncertainties.alternatives: I report it AFTER the dedup block and immediately before `return last;`. Placement relative to the dedup is irrelevant (the dedup does not read `vertices`), but it MUST be after the insertNode loops, which do read it.
uncertainties.confidence: high

uncertainties.alternatives: (a) `(cx-px)*(ay-py) - (ax-px)*(cy-py) >= 0 && ...` (what I reported); (b) `(cx-px)*(ay-py) >= (ax-px)*(cy-py) && ...` as in earcut.js 3.0. If the C++ header was refreshed from JS 3.0 after Aug 2022, (b) would apply and a `pointInTriangleExceptFirst` helper would also exist, called from isEar/isEarHashed with the ear's own prev/next. The two forms differ in last-bit rounding and can therefore differ in output on degenerate data.
uncertainties.confidence: ~85% that released 2.2.4 uses form (a) with no ExceptFirst helper. If your reference build is 'latest master' rather than the 2.2.4 tag, verify this one function first — it is the single most likely divergence in this subsystem.
uncertainties.what: Whether earcut.hpp 2.2.4's pointInTriangle uses the subtracted `>= 0` form or the product-vs-product `>=` form.

uncertainties.alternatives: earcut.js definitely has it. I believe the C++ header omits it and has only `if (!end) end = start;`. Adding it is behavior-preserving for all in-tree call sites, so it cannot change emitted triangles — only crash behavior on a null argument.
uncertainties.confidence: ~70% that C++ omits it; zero impact on output either way.
uncertainties.what: Presence of a leading `if (!start) return start;` in the C++ filterPoints.

uncertainties.alternatives: `std::max<double>(p->x, r->x)` (explicit template arg, what I reported) vs plain `std::max(p->x, r->x)`. Purely cosmetic — both compile to the same comparison and are IEEE-identical for non-NaN doubles.
uncertainties.confidence: ~75% on the explicit <double>; no semantic impact.
uncertainties.what: Exact spelling of the min/max calls in onSegment.

uncertainties.alternatives: The pairing could have been written with the clauses swapped: `(equals(p1,q2) && equals(p2,q1)) || (equals(p1,q1) && equals(p2,q2))`. The predicate is symmetric so the result is identical; only source appearance differs.
uncertainties.confidence: ~90% on the clause content; the clause ORDER has no observable effect.
uncertainties.what: Exact clause order of the older (pre-2.2) `intersects` equals-endpoints guard.

uncertainties.alternatives: It is definitely present in 2.2.x and absent in the early 2.0 line; the precise introduction point is fuzzy. Since it is logically implied by the crossing test for finite coordinates, it only matters for NaN/infinite inputs.
uncertainties.confidence: High that it is present in 2.2.4 (the port target); low on the exact version where it landed.
uncertainties.what: Whether the `p->next->y != p->y` guard in middleInside first appeared in 2.2.0 exactly, versus a 2.1.x patch release.

uncertainties.alternatives: Older earcut.hpp (0.12-era) carried a `bool zOrderComputed` flag; 2.2.x computes z eagerly in indexCurve and has only `int32_t z = 0;`. This belongs to the z-order/hashing subsystem, but removeNode touches prevZ/nextZ so I flag it here.
uncertainties.confidence: ~85% that 2.2.4 has only `int32_t z = 0;` with no computed-flag.
uncertainties.what: The `int32_t` type of Node::z and whether a separate `bool zOrderComputed` field exists.

uncertainties.alternatives: I reported `bool isValidDiagonal(Node* a, Node* b)` (non-const params) while the pure predicates take `const Node*`. Some versions mark pointInTriangle and area `const` members and leave the rest non-const, as I described. This is compile-time only and cannot affect output.
uncertainties.confidence: Medium on the exact const-qualification pattern; zero impact on results.
uncertainties.what: Const-qualification of the member functions and their parameters.

Whether the bbox-containment pre-check (`p->x >= minTX && p->x <= maxTX && ...`) exists inside the loops of isEarHashed, and whether isEarHashed uses the modern simultaneous bidirectional walk or the older two-sequential-loops form.
uncertainties.alternatives: Modern (earcut 2.2.3+ / earcut.hpp master, what I reported): simultaneous `while (p && p->z >= minZ && n && n->z <= maxZ)` plus two tail loops, bbox pre-check present in all three. Older (earcut <= 2.1.x / earcut.hpp <= ~0.12): two sequential loops, first nextZ ascending with `p->z <= maxZ`, then prevZ descending with `p->z >= minZ`, NO bbox pre-check. Both forms compute the same boolean, so the emitted triangle sequence is IDENTICAL either way — this is a performance-only divergence. If byte-identity is the goal you can safely pick either.
uncertainties.confidence: High that the modern form is what current earcut.hpp master contains; certain that the choice does not affect output.

uncertainties.what: Exact spelling of the identity guards in the simultaneous loop: `p != a && p != c` vs `p != ear->prev && p != ear->next`, and whether the identity checks precede or follow the bbox checks.
uncertainties.alternatives: JS 2.2.4 writes bbox-then-`p !== a && p !== c` in the simultaneous loop and `p !== ear.prev && p !== ear.next`-then-bbox in the tail loops. earcut.hpp may spell both as `ear->prev`/`ear->next` throughout. Since a == ear->prev and c == ear->next and all conjuncts are side-effect-free, every ordering is observationally equivalent.
uncertainties.confidence: High that it is semantically irrelevant; medium on the literal source spelling.

uncertainties.what: Whether earcutLinked declares an unused `int iterations = 0; iterations++;` counter.
uncertainties.alternatives: Some revisions of earcut.hpp carried a loop counter that was incremented but never read (a leftover). Present or absent, it has zero effect on output. I omitted it.
uncertainties.confidence: Medium; no output impact.

uncertainties.what: Whether the C++ member is named `inv_size` (snake) or `invSize`, and whether zOrder's parameters are `const double x_, const double y_`.
uncertainties.alternatives: earcut.hpp uses snake_case `inv_size` (unusual for the file, but I am fairly confident) with the trailing-underscore parameter names `x_`/`y_` to avoid shadowing the local `x`/`y`. Naming only; no semantic impact.
uncertainties.confidence: Medium-high; cosmetic.

uncertainties.what: The exact threshold constant and comparison for enabling hashing.
uncertainties.alternatives: I reported `int threshold = 80;` decremented by each ring's size while `threshold >= 0`, then `hashing = threshold < 0`. This means hashing turns on strictly above 80 total vertices. An alternative reading some ports use is a direct `len > 80` test; these differ only at exactly 80/81 boundary semantics for multi-ring input (the short-circuiting loop stops early, so with many rings the decrement form is what matters). I am confident in the decrement form and the value 80.
uncertainties.confidence: High on 80 and on `hashing = threshold < 0`.

uncertainties.what: Whether `Node::z` is `int32_t` initialized to 0 (C++) versus `null` (JS), affecting the `p->z ? p->z : zOrder(...)` idiom.
uncertainties.alternatives: C++ uses `int32_t z = 0;` and the ternary; JS 2.2.4 uses `this.z = 0` with `if (p.z === 0) p.z = zOrder(...)`, and JS 2.1.x used `null` with `p.z === null`. All three behave the same except for the pathological point whose true z is 0 (the bbox min corner), which the C++/modern-JS form recomputes redundantly — same value, no output difference.
uncertainties.confidence: High.

uncertainties.what: Whether sortLinked is declared to return Node* and whether indexCurve discards it.
uncertainties.alternatives: It returns Node* (the new head) and indexCurve calls it as a bare statement, discarding the result. Some compilers warn; the library does not mark it nodiscard. Behaviorally settled: nothing reads the head.
uncertainties.confidence: High.

uncertainties.what: Exact release-number attribution of each change within the C++ earcut.hpp tag history (which of 2.1.0 / 2.1.1 / 2.1.2 / 2.1.3 / 2.1.4 / 2.1.5 / 2.2.0 / 2.2.1 / 2.2.2 / 2.2.3 / 2.2.4 first shipped each delta).
uncertainties.alternatives: I am confident about WHICH variant the reference contains (read from machine code) and confident about the OLD-vs-NEW pairing, but the precise tag boundaries are recalled, not verified. My best mapping: sign/onSegment intersects + zOrder inv_size arrived in the 2.2.0 line; eliminateHole-returns-Node, sectorContainsSector, and the isValidDiagonal opposite-facing-sectors clause arrived in the 2.2.3/2.2.4 line; getLeftmost's y tie-break and the degenerate-hole steiner marking arrived in the 2.1.x line. Treat the OLD/NEW pseudocode pairs as reliable and the version labels as approximate.
uncertainties.confidence: High on variant identity and on old/new pairing; medium-low on exact tag numbers.

uncertainties.what: Whether cureLocalIntersections ever ended with `return p;` instead of `return filterPoints(p, nullptr);` in an early 2.0.x release.
uncertainties.alternatives: Reference definitively has `return filterPoints(p, nullptr)` (tail jump to filterPoints at 0x402b1c with end=nullptr). The claim that an older variant returned p bare is my weakest historical assertion in this report; it may never have existed. It does not affect the reimplementation, only the completeness of the archaeology.
uncertainties.confidence: Low on the historical variant; certain on the reference form.

uncertainties.what: Whether a 3.x release of the C++ port mapbox/earcut.hpp exists.
uncertainties.alternatives: I believe v2.2.4 is the final C++ tag and that 3.0.0 (Nov 2024) is a JS-only, ESM-rewrite release. I have listed the JS 3.0 deltas (compareXYSlope, pointInTriangleExceptFirst, isEar bbox, dropped prev/next guards in isEarHashed) as things to explicitly NOT implement. If a C++ 3.x does exist, those four are the deltas to check first. Either way it is moot for this task: the reference binary is unambiguously pre-3.0.
uncertainties.confidence: Medium on the non-existence of C++ 3.x; high that the reference is pre-3.0.

uncertainties.what: Whether the hashing threshold was ever a value other than 80, or based on a different metric, before 2.0.0.
uncertainties.alternatives: 80 is verified in the reference (mov $0x50) and I believe it has been 80 across the whole 2.x line, matching JS's `data.length > 80 * dim`. Pre-2.0 earcut (1.x) may have used a different heuristic or a node-count metric; I could not verify this and it is out of the requested range.
uncertainties.confidence: High for 2.0.0-2.2.4; unknown for 1.x.

uncertainties.what: The precise semantics of ObjectPool::reset / the 256-element floor and the heap-allocated pool object observed at Earcut+0x50 in this build.
uncertainties.alternatives: The disassembly shows nodes.reset(max(len*3/2, 256)) against a pool reached through a pointer, which does not match my recollection of stock earcut.hpp's inline ObjectPool member. This is allocation strategy only and cannot affect the emitted index sequence (node identity is by pointer, and no output path depends on pool addresses or block boundaries), so I did not chase it further. Flagging in case the parent sees unexpected allocator symbols.
uncertainties.confidence: High that it is output-irrelevant; low on the exact ObjectPool source form.
